entries.fe317bd9c2a833231e924b90e64caa4b0768a826: <div sID="gen10324" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Ps.2" sID="Ps.2"/> <div eID="gen10324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10325" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10326" type="x-p"/> As the foregoing psalm was moral, and showed us our duty, so this is evangelical, and shows us our Saviour. Under the type of David's kingdom (which was of divine appointment, met with much opposition, but prevailed at last) the kingdom of the Messiah, the Son of David, is prophesied of, which is the primary intention and scope of the psalm; and I think there is less in it of the type, and more of the anti-type, than in any of the gospel psalms, for there is nothing in it but what is applicable to Christ, but some things that are not at all applicable to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6-Ps.2.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>): "Thou art my Son" (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">ver. 8</reference>), "I will give thee the uttermost parts of the earth," and (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">ver. 12</reference>), "Kiss the Son." It is interpreted of Christ <reference osisRef="Acts.4.24">Acts iv. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">xiii. 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.5">Heb. i. 5</reference>. The Holy Ghost here foretels, I. The opposition that should be given to the kingdom of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The baffling and chastising of that opposition, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4-Ps.2.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. The setting up of the kingdom of Christ, notwithstanding that opposition, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">ver. 6</reference>. IV. The confirmation and establishment of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">ver. 7</reference>. V. A promise of the enlargement and success of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8-Ps.2.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. VI. A call and exhortation to kings and princes to yield themselves the willing subjects of this kingdom,, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10-Ps.2.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. Or thus: We have here, I. Threatenings denounced against the adversaries of Christ's kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. Promises made to Christ himself, the head of this kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7-Ps.2.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. III. Counsel given to all to espouse the interests of this kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10-Ps.2.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. This psalm, as the former, is very fitly prefixed to this book of devotions, because, as it is necessary to our acceptance with God that we should be subject to the precepts of his law, so it is likewise that we should be subject to the grace of his gospel, and come to him in the name of a Mediator.
entries.3ccd462a71a0a3589a6dde3c194a35c75f38e04d: <div eID="gen10326" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10325" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Enemies of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen10327" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing? <hi type="super">2</hi> The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and against his anointed, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> <hi type="super">3</hi> Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us. <hi type="super">4</hi> He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure. <hi type="super">6</hi> Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion. <div eID="gen10327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10328" type="x-p"/> We have here a very great struggle about the kingdom of Christ, hell and heaven contesting it; the seat of the war is this earth, where Satan has long had a usurped kingdom and exercised dominion to such a degree that he has been called <hi type="italic">the prince of the power of the</hi> very <hi type="italic">air</hi> we breathe in and <hi type="italic">the god of the world</hi> we live in. He knows very well that, as the Messiah's kingdom rises and gets ground, his falls and loses ground; and therefore, though it will be set up certainly, it shall not be set up tamely. Observe here, <div eID="gen10328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10329" type="x-p"/> I. The mighty opposition that would be given to the Messiah and his kingdom, to his holy religion and all the interests of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3">v. 1-3</reference>. One would have expected that so great a blessing to this world would be universally welcomed and embraced, and that every sheaf would immediately bow to that of the Messiah and all the crowns and sceptres on earth would be laid at his feet; but it proves quite contrary. Never were the notions of any sect of philosophers, though ever so absurd, nor the powers of any prince or state, though ever so tyrannical, opposed with so much violence as the doctrine and government of Christ—a sign that it was from heaven, for the opposition was plainly from hell originally. <div eID="gen10329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10330" type="x-p"/> 1. We are here told who would appear as adversaries to Christ and the devil's instruments in this opposition to his kingdom. Princes and people, court and country, have sometimes separate interests, but here they are united against Christ; not the mighty only, but the mob, the <hi type="italic">heathen,</hi> the <hi type="italic">people,</hi> numbers of them, communities of them; though usually fond of liberty, yet they were averse to the liberty Christ came to procure and proclaim. Not the mob only, but the mighty (among whom one might have expected more sense and consideration) appear violent against Christ. Though his kingdom is not of this world, nor in the least calculated to weaken their interests, but very likely, if they pleased, to strengthen them, yet the kings of the earth and rulers are up in arms immediately. See the effects of the old enmity in the seed of the serpent against the seed of the woman, and how general and malignant the corruption of mankind is. See how formidable the enemies of the church are; they are numerous; they are potent. The unbelieving Jews are here called <hi type="italic">heathen,</hi> so wretchedly had they degenerated from the faith and holiness of their ancestors; they stirred up the heathen, the Gentiles, to persecute the Christians. As the Philistines and their lords, Saul and his courtiers, the disaffected party and their ringleaders, opposed David's coming to the crown, so Herod and Pilate, the Gentiles and the Jews, did their utmost against Christ and his interest in men, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.27">Acts iv. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen10330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10331" type="x-p"/> 2. Who it is that they quarrel with, and muster up all their forces against; it is <hi type="italic">against the Lord and against his anointed,</hi> that is, against all religion in general and the Christian religion in particular. It is certain that all who are enemies to Christ, whatever they pretend, are enemies to God himself; they <hi type="italic">have hated both me and my Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.24">John xv. 24</reference>. The great author of our holy religion is here called <hi type="italic">the Lord's anointed,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Messiah,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> in allusion to the anointing of David to be king. He is both authorized and qualified to be the church's head and king, is duly invested in the office and every way fitted for it; yet there are those that are against him; nay, <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they are against him, because they are impatient of God's authority, envious at Christ's advancement, and have a rooted enmity to the Spirit of holiness. <div eID="gen10331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10332" type="x-p"/> 3. The opposition they give is here described. (1.) It is a most spiteful and malicious opposition. They <hi type="italic">rage</hi> and fret; they gnash their teeth for vexation at the setting up of Christ's kingdom; it creates them the utmost uneasiness, and fills them with indignation, so that they have no enjoyment of themselves; see <reference osisRef="Luke.13.14">Luke xiii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.11.47">John xi. 47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.17 Acts.5.33">Acts v. 17, 33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.19.28">xix. 28</reference>. Idolaters raged at the discovery of their folly, the chief priests and Pharisees at the eclipsing of their glory and the shaking of their usurped dominion. Those that did evil raged at the light. (2.) It is a deliberate and politic opposition. They <hi type="italic">imagine</hi> or meditate, that is, they contrive means to suppress the rising interests of Christ's kingdom and are very confident of the success of their contrivances; they promise themselves that they shall run down religion and carry the day. (3.) It is a resolute and obstinate opposition. They <hi type="italic">set themselves,</hi> set their faces as a flint and their hearts as an adamant, in defiance of reason, and conscience, and all the terrors of the Lord; they are proud and daring, like the Babel-builders, and will persist in their resolution, come what will. (4.) It is a combined and confederate opposition. They <hi type="italic">take counsel together,</hi> to assist and animate one another in this opposition; they carry their resolutions <hi type="italic">nemine contradicente—unanimously,</hi> that they will push on the unholy war against the Messiah with the utmost vigour: and thereupon councils are called, cabals are formed, and all their wits are at work to find out ways and means for the preventing of the establishment of Christ's kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.5">Ps. lxxxiii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen10332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10333" type="x-p"/> 4. We are here told what it is they are exasperated at and what they aim at in this opposition (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let us break their bands asunder.</hi> They will not be under any government; they are children of Belial, that cannot endure the yoke, at least the yoke of the Lord and his anointed. They will be content to entertain such notions of the kingdom of God and the Messiah as will serve them to dispute of and to support their own dominion with: if the Lord and his anointed will make them rich and great in the world, they will bid them welcome; but if they will restrain their corrupt appetites and passions, regulate and reform their hearts and lives, and bring them under the government of a pure and heavenly religion, truly then <hi type="italic">they will not have this man to reign over them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.14">Luke xix. 14</reference>. Christ has <hi type="italic">bands and cords</hi> for us; those that will be saved by him must be ruled by him; but they are <hi type="italic">cords of a man,</hi> agreeable to right reason, and <hi type="italic">bands of love,</hi> conducive to our true interest: and yet against those the quarrel is. Why do men oppose religion but because they are impatient of its restraints and obligations? They would break asunder the bands of conscience they are under and the cords of God's commandments by which they are called to tie themselves out from all sin and to themselves up to all duty; they will not receive them, but cast them away as far from them as they can. <div eID="gen10333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10334" type="x-p"/> 5. They are here reasoned with concerning it, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">v. 1</reference>. Why do they do this? (1.) They can show no good cause for opposing so just, holy, and gracious a government, which will not interfere with the secular powers, nor introduce any dangerous principles hurtful to kings or provinces; but, on the contrary, if universally received, would bring a heaven upon earth. (2.) They can hope for no good success in opposing so powerful a kingdom, with which they are utterly unable to contend. It is <hi type="italic">a vain thing;</hi> when they have done their worst Christ will have a church in the world and that church shall be glorious and triumphant. It is <hi type="italic">built upon a rock, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.</hi> The moon walks in brightness, though the dogs bark at it. <div eID="gen10334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10335" type="x-p"/> II. The mighty conquest gained over all this threatening opposition. If heaven and earth be the combatants, it is easy to foretel which will be the conqueror. Those that make this mighty struggle are the people of the earth, and the kings of the earth, who, being of the earth, are earthy; but he whom they contest with is one that <hi type="italic">sits in the heavens,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">v. 4</reference>. He is in the heaven, a place of such a vast prospect that he can oversee them all and all their projects; and such is his power that he can overcome them all and all their attempts. He sits there, as one easy and at rest, out of the reach of all their impotent menaces and attempts. There he sits as Judge in all the affairs of the children of men, perfectly secure of the full accomplishment of all his own purposes and designs, in spite of all opposition, <reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">Ps. xxix. 10</reference>. The perfect repose of the Eternal Mind may be our comfort under all the disquietments of our mind. We are tossed on earth, and in the sea, but he sits in the heavens, where he has prepared his throne for judgment; and therefore, <div eID="gen10335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10336" type="x-p"/> 1. The attempts of Christ's enemies are easily ridiculed. God <hi type="italic">laughs</hi> at them as a company of fools. He <hi type="italic">has them,</hi> and all their attempts, <hi type="italic">in derision,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">the virgin, the daughter of Zion, has despised them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa. xxxvii. 22</reference>. Sinners' follies are the just sport of God's infinite wisdom and power; and those attempts of the kingdom of Satan which in our eyes are formidable in his are despicable. Sometimes God is said to <hi type="italic">awake,</hi> and <hi type="italic">arise,</hi> and <hi type="italic">stir up himself,</hi> for the vanquishing of his enemies; here is said to <hi type="italic">sit still</hi> and vanquish them; for the utmost operations of God's omnipotence create no difficulty at all, nor the least disturbance to his eternal rest. <div eID="gen10336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10337" type="x-p"/> 2. They are justly punished, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.5">v. 5</reference>. Though God despises them as impotent, yet he does not therefore wink at them, but is justly displeased with them as impudent and impious, and will make the most daring sinners to know that he is so and to tremble before him. (1.) Their sin is a provocation to him. He is wroth; he is sorely displeased. We cannot expect that God should be reconciled to us, or well pleased in us, but in and through the anointed; and therefore, if we affront and reject him, we sin against the remedy and forfeit the benefit of his interposition between us and God. (2.) His anger will be a vexation to them; if he but speak to them in his wrath, even the breath of his mouth will be their confusion, slaughter, and consumption, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa. xi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2 Thess. ii. 8</reference>. He speaks, and it is done; he speaks in wrath, and sinners are undone. As a word made us, so a word can unmake us again. <hi type="italic">Who knows the power of his anger?</hi> The enemies rage, but cannot vex God. God sits still, and yet vexes them, puts them in to a consternation (as the word is), and brings them to their wits' end: his setting up this kingdom of his Son, in spite of them, is the greatest vexation to them that can be. They were vexatious to Christ's good subjects; but the day is coming when vexation shall be recompensed to them. <div eID="gen10337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10338" type="x-p"/> 3. They are certainly defeated, and all their counsels turned headlong (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion.</hi> David was advanced to the throne, and became master of the strong-hold of Zion, notwithstanding the disturbance given him by the malcontents in his kingdom, and particularly the affronts he received from the garrison of Zion, who taunted him with their blind and their lame, their maimed soldiers, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.6">2 Sam. v. 6</reference>. The Lord Jesus is exalted to the right hand of the Father, has all power both in heaven and in earth, and is head over all things to the church, notwithstanding the restless endeavours of his enemies to hinder his advancement. (1.) Jesus Christ is a King, and is invested by him who is the fountain of power with the dignity and authority of a sovereign prince in the kingdom both of providence and grace. (2.) God is pleased to call him <hi type="italic">his</hi> King, because he is appointed by him, and entrusted for him with the sole administration of government and judgment. He is his King, for he is dear to the Father, and one in whom he is well pleased. (3.) Christ took not this honour to himself, but was called to it, and he that called him owns him: <hi type="italic">I have set him;</hi> his commandment, his commission, he received from the Father. (4.) Being called to this honour, he was confirmed in it; high places (we say) are slippery places, but Christ, being raised, is fixed: "<hi type="italic">I have set him,</hi> I have settled him." (5.) He is set upon <hi type="italic">Zion,</hi> the hill of God's holiness, a type of the gospel church, for on that the temple was built, for the sake of which the whole mount was called <hi type="italic">holy.</hi> Christ's throne is set up in his church, that is, in the hearts of all believers and in the societies they form. The evangelical law of Christ is said to <hi type="italic">go forth from Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.2">Mic. iv. 2</reference>), and therefore that is spoken of as the head-quarters of this general, the royal seat of this prince, in whom the children of men shall be joyful. <div eID="gen10338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10339" type="x-p"/> We are to sing <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.6">these verses</reference> with a holy exultation, triumphing over all the enemies of Christ's kingdom (not doubting but they will all of them be quickly made his footstool), and triumphing in Jesus Christ as the great trustee of power; and we are to pray, in firm belief of the assurance here given, "Father in heaven, <hi type="italic">Thy kingdom come;</hi> let thy Son's kingdom come."
entries.3d854bf9eec0adbd67e69f9cc0e66962e4baabab: <div eID="gen10339" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Triumphs of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen10340" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> I will declare the decree: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath said unto me, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my Son; this day have I begotten thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> Ask of me, and I shall give <hi type="italic">thee</hi> the heathen <hi type="italic">for</hi> thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth <hi type="italic">for</hi> thy possession. <hi type="super">9</hi> Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel. <div eID="gen10340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10341" type="x-p"/> We have heard what the kings of the earth have to say against Christ's kingdom, and have heard it gainsaid by him that sits in heaven; let us now hear what the Messiah himself has to say for his kingdom, to make good his claims, and it is what all the powers on earth cannot gainsay. <div eID="gen10341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10342" type="x-p"/> I. The kingdom of the Messiah is founded upon a decree, an eternal decree, of God the Father. It was not a sudden resolve, it was not the trial of an experiment, but the result of the counsels of the divine wisdom and the determinations of the divine will, before all worlds, neither of which can be altered—the <hi type="italic">precept</hi> or <hi type="italic">statute</hi> (so some read it), the <hi type="italic">covenant</hi> or <hi type="italic">compact</hi> (so others), the federal transactions between the Father and the Son concerning man's redemption, represented by the covenant of royalty made with David and his seed, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.3">Ps. lxxxix. 3</reference>. This our Lord Jesus often referred to as that which, all along in his undertaking, he governed himself by; <hi type="italic">This is the will of him that sent me,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.40">John vi. 40</reference>. <hi type="italic">This commandment have I received of my Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.10.18">John x. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.31">xiv. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen10342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10343" type="x-p"/> II. There is a declaration of that decree as far as is necessary for the satisfaction of all those who are called and commanded to yield themselves subjects to this king, and to leave those inexcusable who will not have him to reign over them. The decree was secret; it was what the Father said to the Son, when he possessed him in the beginning of his way, before his works of old; but it is declared by a faithful witness, who had lain in the bosom of the Father from eternity, and came into the world as the prophet of the church, to declare him, <reference osisRef="John.1.18">John i. 18</reference>. The fountain of all being is, without doubt, the fountain of all power; and it is by, from, and under him, that the Messiah claims. He has his right to rule from what Jehovah said to him, by whose word all things were made and are governed. Christ here makes a tow-fold title to his kingdom:—1. A title by inheritance (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee.</hi> This scripture the apostle quotes (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.5">Heb. i. 5</reference>) to prove that Christ has a more excellent name than the angels, but that he <hi type="italic">obtained it by inheritance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">v. 4</reference>. He is the Son of God, not by adoption, but his begotten Son, the only begotten of the Father, <reference osisRef="John.1.14">John i. 14</reference>. And the Father owns him, and will have this declared to the world as the reason why he is constituted King upon the holy hill of Zion; he is therefore unquestionably entitled to, and perfectly qualified for, that great trust. He is the Son of God, and therefore of the same nature with the Father, has in him all the fulness of the godhead, infinite wisdom, power, and holiness. The supreme government of the church is too high an honour and too hard an undertaking for any mere creature; none can be fit for it but he who is <hi type="italic">one with the Father</hi> and was <hi type="italic">from eternity by him as one brought up with him,</hi> thoroughly apprized of all his counsels, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>. He is the Son of God, and therefore dear to him, his beloved Son, in whom he is well pleased; and upon this account we are to receive him as a King; for because <hi type="italic">the Father loveth the Son he hath given all things into his hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.35">John iii. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.20">v. 20</reference>. Being a Son, he is heir of all things, and, the Father having made the worlds by him, it is easy to infer thence that by him also he governs them; for he is the eternal Wisdom and the eternal Word. If God hath said unto him, "<hi type="italic">Thou art my Son,</hi>" it becomes each of us to say to him, "Thou art my Lord, my sovereign." Further, to satisfy us that his kingdom is well-grounded upon his sonship, we are here told what his sonship is grounded on: <hi type="italic">This day have I begotten thee,</hi> which refers both to his eternal generation itself, for it is quoted (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.5">Heb. i. 5</reference>) to prove that he is the <hi type="italic">brightness of his Father's glory and the express image of his person</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.3">v. 3</reference>), and to the evidence and demonstration given of it by his resurrection from the dead, for to that also it is expressly applied by the apostle, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">Acts xiii. 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">He hath raised up Jesus again, as it is written, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee.</hi> It was by the resurrection from the dead, that sign of the prophet Jonas, which was to be the most convincing of all, that he was <hi type="italic">declared to be the Son of God with power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Rom. i. 4</reference>. Christ is said to be the <hi type="italic">first-begotten</hi> and <hi type="italic">first-born from the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Rev. i. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.18">Col. i. 18</reference>. Immediately after his resurrection he entered upon the administration of his mediatorial kingdom; it was then that he said, <hi type="italic">All power is given unto me,</hi> and to that especially he had an eye when he taught his disciples to pray, <hi type="italic">Thy kingdom come.</hi> 2. A title by agreement, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8-Ps.2.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. The agreement is, in short, this: the Son must undertake the office of an intercessor, and, upon that condition, he shall have the honour and power of a universal monarch; see <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, because he made intercession for the transgressors. He shall be a priest upon his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zech. vi. 13</reference>. (1.) The Son must ask. This supposes his putting himself voluntarily into a state of inferiority to the Father, by taking upon him the human nature; for, as God, he was equal in power and glory with the Father and had nothing to ask. It supposes the making of a satisfaction by the virtue of which the intercession must be made, and the paying of a price, on which this large demand was to be grounded; see <reference osisRef="John.17.4-John.17.5">John xvii. 4, 5</reference>. The Son, in asking the heathen for his inheritance, aims, not only at his own honour, but at their happiness in him; so that he intercedes for them, ever lives to do so, and is therefore able to save to the uttermost. (2.) The Father will grant more than to the half of the kingdom, even to the kingdom itself. It is here promised him, [1.] That his government shall be universal: he shall have <hi type="italic">the heathen</hi> for his inheritance, not the Jews only, to whose nation the church had been long confined, but the Gentiles also. Those in <hi type="italic">the uttermost parts of the earth</hi> (as this nation of ours) shall be his <hi type="italic">possession,</hi> and he shall have multitudes of willing loyal subjects among them. Baptized Christians are the possession of the Lord Jesus; they are to him for a name and a praise. God the Father gives them to him when by his Spirit and grave he works upon them to submit their necks to the yoke of the Lord Jesus. This is in part fulfilled; a great part of the Gentile world received the gospel when it was first preached, and Christ's throne was set up there where Satan's seat had long been. But it is to be yet further accomplished when <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of this world shall become the kingdoms of the Lord and of his Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Rev. xi. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who shall live when God doeth this?</hi> [2.] That it shall be victorious: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt break them</hi> (those of them that oppose thy kingdom) <hi type="italic">with a rod of iron,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">v. 9</reference>. This was in part fulfilled when the nation of the Jews, those that persisted in unbelief and enmity to Christ's gospel, were destroyed by the Roman power, which was represented (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.40">Dan. ii. 40</reference>) by feet of iron, as here by a rod of iron. It had a further accomplishment in the destruction of the Pagan powers, when the Christian religion came to be established; but it will not be completely fulfilled till all opposing rule, principality, and power, shall be finally put down, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.5-Ps.110.6">Ps. cx. 5, 6</reference>. Observe, How powerful Christ is and how weak the enemies of his kingdom are before him; he has a rod of iron wherewith to crush those that will not submit to his golden sceptre; they are but like a potter's vessel before him, suddenly, easily, and irreparably dashed in pieces by him; see <reference osisRef="Rev.2.27">Rev. ii. 27</reference>. "Thou shalt do it, that is, thou shalt have <hi type="italic">leave</hi> to do it." Nations shall be ruined, rather than the gospel church shall not be built and established. <hi type="italic">I have loved thee, therefore will I give men for thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 4</reference>. "Thou shalt have power to do it; none shall be able to stand before thee; and thou shalt do it effectually." Those that will not bow shall break. <div eID="gen10343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10344" type="x-p"/> In singing this, and praying it over, we must give glory to Christ as the eternal Son of God and our rightful Lord, and must take comfort from this promise, and plead it with God, that the kingdom of Christ shall be enlarged and established and shall triumph over all opposition.
entries.411787f331931a4bc5f948d8b7755e497375c0fc: <div eID="gen10344" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Warning to the Enemies of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen10345" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth. <hi type="super">11</hi> Serve the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with fear, and rejoice with trembling. <hi type="super">12</hi> Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish <hi type="italic">from</hi> the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> all they that put their trust in him. <div eID="gen10345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10346" type="x-p"/> We have here the practical application of this gospel doctrine concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, by way of exhortation to the kings and judges of the earth. They hear that it is in vain to oppose Christ's government; let them therefore be so wise for themselves as to submit to it. He that has power to destroy them shows that he has no pleasure in their destruction, for he puts them into a way to make themselves happy, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10">v. 10</reference>. Those that would be wise must be instructed; and those are truly wise that receive instruction from the word of God. Kings and judges stand upon a level with common persons before God; and it is as necessary for them to be religious as for any others. Those that give law and judgment to others must receive law from Christ, and it will be their wisdom to do so. What is said to them is said to all, and is required of every one of us, only it is directed to kings and judges because of the influence which their example will have upon their inferiors, and because they were men of rank and power that opposed the setting up of Christ's kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">v. 2</reference>. We are exhorted, <div eID="gen10346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10347" type="x-p"/> I. To reverence God and to stand in awe of him, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.11">v. 11</reference>. This is the great duty of natural religion. God is great, and infinitely above us, just and holy, and provoked against us, and therefore we ought to fear him and tremble before him; yet he is our Lord and Master, and we are bound to serve him, our friend and benefactor, and we have reason to rejoice in him; and these are very well consistent with each other, for, 1. We must serve God in all ordinances of worship, and all instances of a godly conversation, but with a holy fear, a jealousy over ourselves, and a reverence of him. Even kings themselves, whom others serve and fear, must serve and fear God; there is the same indefinite distance between them and God that there is between the meanest of their subjects and him. 2. We must rejoice in God, and, in subordination to him, we may rejoice in other things, but still with a holy trembling, as those that know what a glorious and jealous God he is, whose eye is always upon us. Our salvation must be wrought out <hi type="italic">with fear and trembling,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.12">Phil. ii. 12</reference>. We ought to rejoice in the setting up of the kingdom of Christ, but to <hi type="italic">rejoice with trembling,</hi> with a holy awe of him, a holy fear for ourselves, lest we come short, and a tender concern for the many precious souls to whom his gospel and kingdom are a savour of death unto death. Whatever we rejoice in, in this world, it must always be with trembling, lest we grow vain in our joy and be puffed up with the things we rejoice in, and because of the uncertainty of them and the damp which by a thousand accidents may soon be cast upon our joy. To <hi type="italic">rejoice with trembling is to rejoice as though we rejoiced not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.30">1 Cor. vii. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen10347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10348" type="x-p"/> II. To welcome Jesus Christ and to submit to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">v. 12</reference>. This is the great duty of the Christian religion; it is that which is required of all, even kings and judges, and it is our wisdom and interest to do it. Observe here, <div eID="gen10348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10349" type="x-p"/> 1. The command given to this purport: <hi type="italic">Kiss the Son.</hi> Christ is called the <hi type="italic">Son</hi> because so he was declared (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou art my Son.</hi> He is the Son of God by eternal generation, and, upon that account, he is to be adored by us. He is the <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> (that is, the Mediator, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">John v. 27</reference>), and, upon that account, to be received and submitted to. He is called the <hi type="italic">Son,</hi> to include both, as God is often called emphatically the <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> because he is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in him our Father, and we must have an eye to him under both considerations. Our duty to Christ is here expressed figuratively: <hi type="italic">Kiss the Son,</hi> not with a betraying kiss, as Judas kissed him, and as all hypocrites, who pretend to honour him, but really affront him; but with a believing kiss. (1.) With a kiss of agreement and reconciliation. Kiss, and be friends, as Jacob and Esau; let the quarrel between us and God terminate; let the acts of hostility cease, and let us be at peace with God in Christ, who is our peace. (2.) With a kiss of adoration and religious worship. Those that worshipped idols kissed them, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.18">1 Kings xix. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.2">Hos. xiii. 2</reference>. Let us study how to do honour to the Lord Jesus, and to give unto him the glory due unto his name. <hi type="italic">He is thy Lord, and worship thou him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Ps. xlv. 11</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">worship the Lamb,</hi> as well as him that sits on the throne, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9-Rev.5.13">Rev. v. 9-13</reference>. (3.) With a kiss of affection and sincere love: "<hi type="italic">Kiss the Son;</hi> enter into a covenant of friendship with him, and let him be very dear and precious to you; love him above all, love him in sincerity, love him much, as she did to whom much was forgiven, and, in token of it, kissed his feet," <reference osisRef="Luke.7.38">Luke vii. 38</reference>. (4.) With a kiss of allegiance and loyalty, as Samuel kissed Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1">1 Sam. x. 1</reference>. Swear fealty and homage to him, submit to his government, take his yoke upon you, and give up yourselves to be governed by his laws, disposed of by his providence, and entirely devoted to his interest. <div eID="gen10349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10350" type="x-p"/> 2. The reasons to enforce this command; and they are taken from our own interest, which God, in his gospel, shows a concern for. Consider, <div eID="gen10350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10351" type="x-p"/> (1.) The certain ruin we run upon if we refuse and reject Christ: "<hi type="italic">Kiss the Son;</hi> for it is at your peril if you do not." [1.] "It will be a great provocation to him. Do it, <hi type="italic">lest he be angry.</hi>" The Father is angry already; the Son is the Mediator that undertakes to make peace; if we slight him, the <hi type="italic">Father's wrath abides upon us</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.36">John iii. 36</reference>), and not only so, but there is an addition of the Son's wrath too, to whom nothing is more displeasing than to have the offers of his grace slighted and the designs of it frustrated. The Son can be angry, though a Lamb; he is the lion of the tribe of Judah, and the wrath of this king, this King of kings, will be as the roaring of a lion, and will drive even mighty men and chief captains to seek in vain for shelter in rocks and mountains, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Rev. vi. 16</reference>. If the Son be angry, who shall intercede for us? There remains no more sacrifice, no other name by which we can be saved. Unbelief is a sin against the remedy. [2.] It will be utter destruction to yourselves: <hi type="italic">Lest you perish from the way,</hi> or <hi type="italic">in</hi> the way so some, <hi type="italic">in</hi> the way of your sins, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> the way of your vain hopes; <hi type="italic">lest your way perish</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Ps. i. 6</reference>), lest you prove to have missed the way to happiness. Christ is the way; take heed lest you be cut off from him as your way to God. It intimates that they were, or at least thought themselves, in the way; but, by neglecting Christ, they perished from it, which aggravates their ruin, that they go to hell from the way to heaven, are not far from the kingdom of God and yet never arrive there. <div eID="gen10351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10352" type="x-p"/> (2.) The happiness we are sure of if we yield ourselves to Christ. When his wrath is kindled, though <hi type="italic">but a little,</hi> the least spark of that fire is enough to make the proudest sinner miserable if it fasten upon his conscience; for it will burn to the lowest hell: one would think it should therefore follow, "When his wrath is kindled, woe be to those that despise him;" but the Psalmist startles at the thought, deprecates that dreadful doom and pronounces those blessed that escape it. Those that trust in him, and so kiss him, are truly happy; but they will especially appear to be so when the wrath of Christ is kindled against others. Blessed will those be in the day of wrath, who, by trusting in Christ, have made him their refuge and patron; when the hearts of others fail them for fear they shall lift up their heads with joy; and then those who now despise Christ and his followers will be forced to say, to their own greater confusion, "Now we see that <hi type="italic">blessed are all those,</hi> and those only, <hi type="italic">that trust in him.</hi>" <div eID="gen10352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10353" type="x-p"/> In singing this, and praying it over, we should have our hearts filled with a holy awe of God, but at the same time borne up with a cheerful confidence in Christ, in whose mediation we may comfort and encourage ourselves and one another. <hi type="italic">We are the circumcision, that rejoice in Christ Jesus.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.2"/> <div eID="gen10353" type="x-p"/>

entries.efe6c6ab4a59c2edabb453796e1587a98974066f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5461"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12">Psa 2:1-12</reference>. The number and authorship of this Psalm are stated (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.25">Ac 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">13:33</reference>). Though the warlike events of David's reign may have suggested its imagery, the scenes depicted and the subjects presented can only find a fulfilment in the history and character of Jesus Christ, to which, as above cited and in <reference osisRef="Heb.1.5">He 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">5:5</reference>, the New Testament writers most distinctly testify. In a most animated and highly poetical style, the writer, in "four stanzas of three verses each," sets forth the inveterate and furious, though futile, hostility of men to God and His anointed, God's determination to carry out His purpose, that purpose as stated more fully by His Son, the establishment of the Mediatorial kingdom, and the imminent danger of all who resist, as well as the blessing of all who welcome this mighty and triumphant king.</title> <div sID="gen8252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5461"/><hi type="bold">1. Why do the heathen, &c.--</hi>Beholding, in prophetic vision, the peoples and nations, as if in a tumultuous assembly, raging with a fury like the raging of the sea, designing to resist God's government, the writer breaks forth into an exclamation in which are mingled surprise at their folly, and indignation at their rebellion.<div eID="gen8252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heathen--</hi>nations generally, not as opposed to Jews.<div eID="gen8253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the people--</hi>or, literally, "peoples," or races of men. <div eID="gen8254" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb7fc3402d7f0d38c1c5eb6754dc85f8c492305a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5462"/><div sID="gen8255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5462"/>2. The kings and rulers lead on their subjects.<div eID="gen8255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set themselves--</hi>take a stand.<div eID="gen8256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take counsel--</hi>literally, "sit together," denoting their deliberation.<div eID="gen8257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anointed--</hi>Hebrew, "Messiah"; Greek, "Christ" (<reference osisRef="John.1.41">Joh 1:41</reference>). Anointing, as an emblem of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, was conferred on prophets (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">Is 6:1</reference>); priests (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.30">Ex 30:30</reference>); and kings (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1">1Sa 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">16:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.39">1Ki 1:39</reference>). Hence this title well suited Him who holds all these offices, and was generally used by the Jews before His coming, to denote Him (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>). While the prophet has in view men's opposition generally, he here depicts it in its culminating aspect as seen in the events of Christ's great trial. Pilate and Herod, and the rulers of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.1">Mt 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.1-Luke.23.25">Lu 23:1-25</reference>), with the furious mob, are vividly portrayed. <div eID="gen8258" type="x-p"/>
entries.84a3c9a5804369c9b49a226af27b921b1531dc54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5463"/><div sID="gen8259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5463"/>3. The rebellious purposes of men are more distinctly announced by this representation of their avowal in words, as well as actions.<div eID="gen8259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bands ... and ... cords--</hi>denote the restraints of government. <div eID="gen8260" type="x-p"/>
entries.89ffd951ac766cb788654544cca354b1327e7926: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5464"/><div sID="gen8261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5464"/>4. By a figure whose boldness is only allowable to an inspired writer, God's conduct and language in view of this opposition are now related.<div eID="gen8261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He that sitteth in the heavens--</hi>enthroned in quiet dignities (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">Psa 29:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Is 40:22</reference>).<div eID="gen8262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall laugh--</hi>in supreme contempt; their vain rage excites His derision. He is still the Lord, literally, "Sovereign," though they rebel. <div eID="gen8263" type="x-p"/>
entries.e68ae9620e6da5dd837dc599c996c4c8438857d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5465"/><div sID="gen8264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5465"/><hi type="bold">5. Then shall he speak--</hi>His righteous indignation as well as contempt is roused. For God to speak is for Him to act, for what He resolves He will do (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.3">Ge 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.9">Psa 33:9</reference>).<div eID="gen8264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vex them--</hi>agitate or terrify them (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.15">Psa 83:15</reference>). <div eID="gen8265" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a1a86531182a06ce0b84109cca89987d787c98a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5466"/><div sID="gen8266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5466"/>6. The purpose here declared, in its execution, involves their overthrow.<div eID="gen8266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Yet--</hi>literally, "and," in an adversative sense.<div eID="gen8267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have set--</hi>anointed, or firmly placed, with allusion in the Hebrew to "casting an image in a mould." The sense is not materially varied in either case.<div eID="gen8268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my king--</hi>appointed by Me and for Me (<reference osisRef="Num.27.18">Nu 27:18</reference>).<div eID="gen8269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon my holy hill of Zion--</hi>Zion, selected by David as the abode of the ark and the seat of God's visible residence (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.1">1Ki 8:1</reference>); as also David, the head of the Church and nation, and type of Christ, was called holy, and the Church itself came to be thus named (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.11">Psa 9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.18">51:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.99.2">99:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.18">Is 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">18:7</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen8270" type="x-p"/>
entries.db3a2d0a33969a67d1f6ec0471693970421d61e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5467"/><div sID="gen8271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5467"/>7. The king thus constituted declares the fundamental law of His kingdom, in the avowal of His Sonship, a relation involving His universal dominion.<div eID="gen8271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this day have I begotten thee--</hi>as <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2Sa 7:14</reference>, "he shall be My son," is a solemn recognition of this relation. The interpretation of this passage to describe the inauguration of Christ as Mediatorial King, by no means impugns the Eternal Sonship of His divine nature. In <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">Ac 13:33</reference>, Paul's quotation does not imply an application of this passage to the resurrection; for "raised up" in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.32">Ac 13:32</reference> is used as in <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>; 3:22, &c., to denote bringing Him into being as a man; and not that of resurrection, which it has only when, as in <reference osisRef="Acts.2.34">Ac 2:34</reference>, allusion is made to His death (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>). That passage says He was declared as to His divine nature to be the Son of God, by the resurrection, and only teaches that that event manifested a truth already existing. A similar recognition of His Sonship is introduced in <reference osisRef="Heb.5.5">He 5:5</reference>, by these ends, and by others in <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">17:5</reference>. <div eID="gen8272" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6f8b12deef09211d4bf1fdef0a66f78d31ff1be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5468"/><div sID="gen8273" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5468"/>8. The hopes of the rebels are thus overthrown, and not only so; the kingdom they opposed is destined to be coextensive with the earth.<div eID="gen8273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heathen--</hi>or, "nations" (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Psa 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen8274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8275" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the uttermost parts of the earth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.22.27">Psa 22:27</reference>); denotes universality. <div eID="gen8275" type="x-p"/>
entries.b382712034ab1b6ebe2626dda37ac186195b0e48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5469"/><div sID="gen8276" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5469"/>9. His enemies shall be subject to His terrible power (<reference osisRef="Job.4.9">Job 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>), as His people to His grace (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen8276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rod of iron--</hi>denotes severity (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.27">Re 2:27</reference>).<div eID="gen8277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a potter's vessel--</hi>when shivered cannot be mended, which will describe utter destruction. <div eID="gen8278" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0f6d01bdfbc5aeb07d80a46e47e61673ee3384b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5470"/><div sID="gen8279" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5470"/><hi type="bold">10-12. kings ... judges--</hi>For rulers generally (<reference osisRef="Ps.148.11">Psa 148:11</reference>), who have been leaders in rebellion, should be examples of penitent submission, and with fear for His terrible judgments, mingled with trust in His mercy, acknowledge-- <div eID="gen8279" type="x-p"/>

entries.a3ba23e23f3707de0026174a3782789b9040de1b: <div eID="gen18291" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18292" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18293" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18293" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18292" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18294" type="x-p"/> This Psalm treats of the opposition raised, both by Jew and Gentile, against the kingdom of Christ, <reference osisRef="Psa.2.1-Psa.2.3">Psa 2:1-3</reference>. Christ's victory, and the confusion of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.2.4-Psa.2.6">Psa 2:4-6</reference>. The promulgation of the Gospel after his resurrection, <reference osisRef="Psa.2.7-Psa.2.9">Psa 2:7-9</reference>. A call to all the potentates and judges of the earth to accept it, because of the destruction that shall fall on those who reject it, <reference osisRef="Psa.2.10-Psa.2.12">Psa 2:10-12</reference>. <div eID="gen18294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18295" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18296" type="x-p"/> Why do the heathen rage - It has been supposed that David composed this Psalm after he had taken Jerusalem from the Jebusites, and made it the head of the kingdom; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.7-2Sam.5.9">2Sam 5:7-9</reference>. The Philistines, hearing this, encamped in the valley of Rephaim, nigh to Jerusalem, and Josephus, Antiq. lib. 7: c. 4, says that all Syria, Phoenicia, and the other circumjacent warlike people, united their armies to those of the Philistines, in order to destroy David before he had strengthened himself in the kingdom. David, having consulted the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.17-2Sam.5.19">2Sam 5:17-19</reference>, gave them battle, and totally overthrew the whole of his enemies. In the first place, therefore, we may suppose that this Psalm was written to celebrate the taking of Jerusalem, and the overthrow of all the kings and chiefs of the neighboring nations. In the second place we find from the use made of this Psalm by the apostles, <reference osisRef="Act.4.27">Act 4:27</reference>, that David typified Jesus Christ; and that the Psalm celebrates the victories of the Gospel over the Philistine Jews, and all the confederate power of the heathen governors of the Roman empire. <div eID="gen18296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18297" type="x-p"/> The heathen, גוים goyim, the nations; those who are commonly called the Gentiles. <div eID="gen18297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18298" type="x-p"/> Rage, רגשו rageshu, the gnashing of teeth, and tumultuously rushing together, of those indignant and cruel people, are well expressed by the sound as well as the meaning of the original word. A vain thing. Vain indeed to prevent the spread of the Gospel in the world. To prevent Jesus Christ, the King of kings, and Lord of lords, from having the empire of his own earth. So vain were their endeavors that every effort only tended to open and enlarge the way for the all-conquering sway of the scepter of righteousness.
entries.de8c18a1ea6ce248e70dea660d932cc4994be84c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18299" type="x-p"/> Against his anointed - על משיחיה al Meshichiah, "Against his Messiah." - Chaldee. But as this signifies the anointed person, it may refer first to David, as it does secondly to Christ.
entries.ff8b410ca1e9eb164ff53e1267904cd7a136df04: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18300" type="x-p"/> Let us break their bands - These are the words of the confederate heathen powers; and here, as Bishop Horne well remarks, "we may see the ground of opposition; namely, the unwillingness of rebellious nature to submit to the obligations of Divine laws, which cross the interests, and lay a restraint on the desires of men. Corrupt affections are the most inveterate enemies of Christ, and their language is, We will not have this man to reign over us. Doctrines would be readily believed if they involved in them no precepts; and the Church may be tolerated in the world if she will only give up her discipline."
entries.d04fe6c006659dcdff8c55a27bb0600c3f13a489: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18301" type="x-p"/> He that sitteth in the heavens - Whose kingdom ruleth over all, and is above all might and power, human and diabolical. Shall laugh. Words spoken after the manner of men; shall utterly contemn their puny efforts; shall beat down their pride, assuage their malice, and confound their devices.
entries.d3b4727a8e047afb3d404ea33668eb59fd9646f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18302" type="x-p"/> Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath - He did so to the Jews who rejected the Gospel, and vexed and ruined them by the Roman armies; he did so with the opposing Roman emperors, destroying all the contending factions, till he brought the empire under the dominion of one, and him he converted to Christianity viz., Constantine the Great.
entries.fae31ade24dd76bf896ee64e43cb3ab53feada1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18303" type="x-p"/> I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion - Here the Gospel shall be first preached; here the kingdom of Christ shall be founded; and from hence shall the doctrine of the Lord go out into all the earth.
entries.7ef90cf73d31c3fdba5c8ed68b546683008f4e70: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18304" type="x-p"/> I will declare the decree - These words are supposed to have been spoken by the Messiah. I will declare to the world the decree, the purpose of God to redeem them by my blood, and to sanctify them by my Spirit. My death shall prove that the required atonement has been made; my resurrection shall prove that this atonement has been accepted. <div eID="gen18304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18305" type="x-p"/> Thou art my Son - Made man, born of a woman by the creative energy of the Holy Ghost, that thou mightest feel and suffer for man, and be the first-born of many brethren. <div eID="gen18305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18306" type="x-p"/> This day have I begotten thee - By thy resurrection thou art declared to be the Son of God, εν δυναμει, by miraculous power, being raised from the dead. Thus by thy wondrous and supernatural nativity, most extraordinary death, and miraculous resurrection, thou art declared to be the Son of God. And as in that Son dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, all the sufferings and the death of that human nature were stamped with an infinitely meritorious efficacy. We have St. Paul's authority for applying to the resurrection of our Lord these words, "Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee;" - see <reference osisRef="Act.13.33">Act 13:33</reference>; see also <reference osisRef="Heb.5.6">Heb 5:6</reference>; - and the man must indeed be a bold interpreter of the Scriptures who would give a different gloss to that of the apostle. It is well known that the words, "Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee," have been produced by many as a proof of the eternal generation of the Son of God. On the subject itself I have already given my opinion in my note on <reference osisRef="Luk.1.35">Luk 1:35</reference>, from which I recede not one hair's breadth. Still however it is necessary to spend a few moments on the clause before us. The word היום haiyom, Today, Is in no part of the sacred writings used to express eternity, or any thing in reference to it; nor can it have any such signification. To-day is an absolute designation of the present, and equally excludes time past and time future; and never can, by any figure, or allowable latitude of construction, be applied to express eternity. But why then does the Divine Spirit use the word begotten in reference to the declaration of the inauguration of the Messiah to his kingdom, and his being seated at the right hand of God? Plainly to show both to Jews and Gentiles that this Man of sorrows, this Outcast from society, this Person who was prosecuted as a blasphemer of God, and crucified as an enemy to the public peace and a traitor to the government, is no less than that eternal Word, who was in the beginning with God, who was God, and in whom dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily: that this rejected Person was he for whom in the fullness of time a body was prepared, begotten by the exclusive power of the Most High in the womb of an unspotted virgin, which body he gave unto death as a sin-offering for the redemption of the world; and having raised it from death, declared it to be that miraculously-begotten Son of God, and now gave farther proof of this by raising the God-man to his right hand. <div eID="gen18306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18307" type="x-p"/> The word ילדתי yalidti, "I have begotten," is here taken in the sense of manifesting, exhibiting, or declaring; and to this sense of it St. Paul (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.3">Rom 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Rom 1:4</reference>) evidently alludes when speaking of "Jesus Christ, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, του ὁρισθεντος Υἱου Θεου εν δυναμει, κατα Πνευμα αγιωσυνης, εξ αναστασεως νεκρων; and declared (exhibited or determined) to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness." This very rejected Person, I this day, by raising him from the dead, and placing him at my right hand, giving to him all power in heaven and earth, declare to be my Son, the beloved one in whom I am well pleased. Therefore hear him, believe on him, and obey him; for there is no redemption but through his blood; no salvation but in his name; no resurrection unto eternal life but through his resurrection, ascension, and powerful intercession at my right hand. Thou art my Son; this day have I declared and manifested thee to be such. It was absolutely necessary to the salvation of men, and the credibility of the Gospel, that the supernatural origin of the humanity of Jesus Christ should be manifested and demonstrated. Hence we find the inspired writers taking pains to show that he was born of a woman, and of that woman by the sovereign power of the everlasting God. This vindicated the character of the blessed virgin, showed the human nature of Christ to be immaculate, and that, even in respect to this nature, he was every way qualified to be a proper atoning sacrifice and Mediator between God and man. I need not tell the learned reader that the Hebrew verb ילד yalad, to beget, is frequently used in reference to inanimate things, to signify their production, or the exhibition of the things produced. In <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Gen 2:4</reference> : These are the generations, תולדות toledoth, of the heavens and the earth; this is the order in which God produced and exhibited them. See Hebrews and Eng. Concord., Venema, etc.
entries.85d9dc3023c5c1bff68345ff55720b7259f95575: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18308" type="x-p"/> Ask of me, and I shall give thee - Here a second branch of Christ's office as Savior of the world is referred to; viz., his mediatorial office. Having died as an atoning sacrifice, and risen again from the dead, he was now to make intercession for mankind; and in virtue and on account of what he had done and suffered, he was, at his request, to have the nations for his inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for his possession. He was to become supreme Lord in the mediatorial kingdom; in consequence of which he sent his apostles throughout the habitable globe to preach the Gospel to every man.
entries.adfd95e7a2e7a35d9c4373c24f88e3d66638783a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen18308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18309" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron - This may refer to the Jewish nation, whose final rejection of the Gospel was foreseen, and in whose place the Gentiles or heathen were brought into the Church of Christ. They were dispossessed of their land, their city was razed to its foundations, their temple was burnt with fire, and upwards of a million of themselves were slaughtered by the Romans! So heavily did the iron rod of God's judgments fall upon them for their obstinate unbelief.
entries.56e567e59bfd9cbea559aa5c75d206e8036d73be: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18310" type="x-p"/> Be wise - O ye kings - An exhortation of the Gospel to the rulers of all kingdoms, nations, and states, to whom it may be sent. All these should listen to its maxims, be governed by its precepts, and rule their subjects according to its dictates. <div eID="gen18310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18311" type="x-p"/> Be instructed, ye judges - Rather, Be ye reformed - cast away all your idolatrous maxims; and receive the Gospel as the law, or the basis of the law, of the land.
entries.73b8d233d084b51d512997aeb3bfe167e3e076a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen18311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18312" type="x-p"/> Serve the Lord with fear - A general direction to all men. Fear God with that reverence which is due to his supreme majesty. Serve him as subjects should their sovereign, and as servants should their master. <div eID="gen18312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18313" type="x-p"/> Rejoice with trembling - If ye serve God aright, ye cannot but be happy; but let a continual filial fear moderate all your joys. Ye must all stand at last before the judgment-seat of God; watch, pray, believe, work, and keep humble.
entries.ddfce0e816b8e66c3655e6d3e6abaa858e80e9ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen18313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18314" type="x-p"/> Kiss the Son, lest he be angry - It is remarkable that the word son (בר bar, a Chaldee word) is not found in any of the versions except the Syriac, nor indeed any thing equivalent to it. <div eID="gen18314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18315" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee, Vulgate, Septuagint, Arabic, and Ethiopic, have a term which signifies doctrine or discipline: "Embrace discipline, lest the Lord be angry with you," etc. This is a remarkable case, and especially that in so pure a piece of Hebrew as this poem is, a Chaldee word should have been found; rb bar, instead of b ben, which adds nothing to the strength of the expression or the elegance of the poetry. I know it is supposed that rb bar is also pure Hebrew, as well as Chaldee; but as it is taken in the former language in the sense of purifying, the versions probably understood it so here. Embrace that which is pure; namely, the doctrine of God. <div eID="gen18315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18316" type="x-p"/> As all judgment is committed to the Son, the Jews and others are exhorted to submit to him, to be reconciled to him, that they might be received into his family, and be acknowledged as his adopted children. Kissing was the token of subjection and friendship. <div eID="gen18316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18317" type="x-p"/> Is kindled but a little - The slightest stroke of the iron rod of Christ's justice is sufficient to break in pieces a whole rebel world. Every sinner, not yet reconciled to God through Christ, should receive this as a most solemn warning. <div eID="gen18317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18318" type="x-p"/> Blessed: are all they - He is only the inexorable Judge to them who harden their hearts in their iniquity, and still not come unto him that they may have life. But all they who trust in him - who repose all their trust and confidence in him as their atonement and as their Lord, shall be blessed with innumerable blessings, For as the word is the same here as in <reference osisRef="Psa.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>, אשרי ashrey, it may be translated the same. "O the blessedness of all them who trust in him!" <div eID="gen18318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18319" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is remarkable, not only for its subject - the future kingdom of the Messiah, its rise, opposition, and gradual extent, but also for the elegant change of person. In the first verse the prophet speaks; in the third, the adversaries; in the fourth and fifth, the prophet answers, in the sixth, Jehovah speaks; in the seventh, the Messiah; in the eighth and ninth, Jehovah answers, and in the tenth to the twelfth, the prophet exhorts the opponents to submission and obedience - Dr. A. Bayly. <div eID="gen18319" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">ANALYSIS OF THE SECOND PSALM</title> <div sID="gen18320" type="x-p"/> The prime subject of this Psalm is CHRIST; the type, DAVID. The persons we are chiefly to reflect on are three, and which make three parts of the Psalm: I. The enemies of Christ; II. Christ the Lord; III. The princes and judges of the earth. <div eID="gen18320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18321" type="x-p"/> I. The enemies of Christ are great men, who are described here, partly from their wickedness, and partly from their weakness. <div eID="gen18321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18322" type="x-p"/> First, Their wickedness is apparent. 1. They furiously rage. 2. They tumultuously assemble. 3. They set themselves-stand up, and take counsel, against the Lord and against his anointed. 4. They encourage themselves in mischief, saying, "Come, and let us cast away their cords from us." All which is sharpened by the interrogatory Why! <div eID="gen18322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18323" type="x-p"/> Secondly, Their weakness; in that they shall never be able to bring their plots and conspiracies against Christ and his kingdom to pass; for, 1. What they imagine is but a vain thing. 2. "He that sits in heaven shall laugh, and have them in derision." 3. "He shall speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure." 4. For, maugre all their plots, "God hath set up his king upon his holy hill of Zion." <div eID="gen18323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18324" type="x-p"/> II. At Ps 2:6 begins the exaltation of Christ to his kingdom, which is the SECOND PART of the Psalm; in which the prophet, by a προσωποποιια, or personification, brings in God the Father speaking, and the Son answering. <div eID="gen18324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18325" type="x-p"/> First, The words of the Father are, "I have set my king;" where we have the inauguration of Christ, or his vocation to the crown. <div eID="gen18325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18326" type="x-p"/> Secondly, The answer of the Son, "I will preach the law;" which sets forth his willing obedience to publish and proclaim the laws of the kingdom; of which the chief is, "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee." <div eID="gen18326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18327" type="x-p"/> Thirdly, The reply of the Father, containing the reward that Christ was to have upon the publication of the Gospel; which was, 1. An addition to his empire by the conversion and accession of the Gentiles: "Ask of me, and I will give thee the heathen for thine inheritance," &c. 2. And the confusion of his enemies: "Thou shalt break them," who would not have thee reign, that did rage and stand up against thee, "with a rod of iron; and break them in pieces as a potter's vessel." <div eID="gen18327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18328" type="x-p"/> III. In the third part the prophet descends to his exhortation and admonition, and that very aptly; for, Is Christ a King? Is he a King anointed by God? Is he a great King, a powerful King? So great that the nations are his subjects? So powerful that he will break and batter to pieces his enemies? Besides, Is he the only begotten Son of God? Be wise, therefore, O ye kings. In this we find, <div eID="gen18328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18329" type="x-p"/> First, The persons to whom this caveat is given: kings and judges. <div eID="gen18329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18330" type="x-p"/> Secondly, What they are taught. 1. To know their duty. "Be wise; be learned." 2. To do their duty: "Serve the Lord with fear; rejoice with trembling; kiss the Son." <div eID="gen18330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18331" type="x-p"/> Thirdly, The time when this is to be done; even now. The reason double: 1. Drawn from his wrath, and the consequent punishment: "Lest he be angry, and ye perish from the right way, when his wrath is kindled but a little." 2. From the happy condition of those who learn to know, and fear, and serve, and adore him: "Blessed are all they that put their trust in him." There must be no delay; this is the time of wrath, and the day of salvation.  <chapter eID="Ps.2"/> <div eID="gen18331" type="x-p"/>

entries.eb502dd10036dc53f4e3070170a174d1e900b590: <div eID="gen9040" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Kingdom of God and of His Christ, to Which Everything Must Bow</title> <div sID="gen9041" type="x-p"/> The didactic <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6">Psa 1:1-6</reference> which began with אשׁרי, is now followed by a prophetic Psalm, which closes with אשׁרי. It coincides also in other respects with <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6">Psa 1:1-6</reference>, but still more with Psalms of the earlier time of the kings (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.9">Psa 59:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.3-Ps.83.9">Psa 83:3-9</reference>) and with Isaiah’s prophetic style. The rising of the confederate nations and their rulers against Jahve and His Anointed will be dashed to pieces against the imperturbable all-conquering power of dominion, which Jahve has entrusted to His King set upon Zion, His Son. This is the fundamental thought, which is worked out with the vivid directness of dramatic representation. The words of the singer and seer begin and end the Psalm. The rebels, Jahve, and His Anointed come forward, and speak for themselves; but the framework is formed by the composer’s discourse, which, like the chorus of the Greek drama, expresses the reflexions and feelings which are produced on the spectators and hearers. The poem before us is not purely lyric. The personality of the poet is kept in the background. The Lord’s Anointed who speaks in the middle of the Psalm is not the anonymous poet himself. It may, however, be a king of the time, who is here regarded in the light of the Messianic promise, or that King of the future, in whom at a future period the mission of the Davidic kingship in the world shall be fulfilled: at all events this Lord’s Anointed comes forward with the divine power and glory, with which the Messiah appears in the prophets. <div eID="gen9041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9042" type="x-p"/> The Psalm is anonymous. For this very reason we may not assign it to David (Hofm.) nor to Solomon (Ew.); for nothing is to be inferred from <reference osisRef="Acts.4.25">Act 4:25</reference>, since in the New Testament “hymn of David” and “psalm” are co-ordinate ideas, and it is always far more hazardous to ascribe an anonymous Psalm to David or Solomon, than to deny to one inscribed לדוד or לשׁלמה direct authorship from David or Solomon. But the subject of the Psalm is neither David (Kurtz) nor Solomon (Bleek). It might be David, for in his reign there is at least one coalition of the peoples like that from which our Psalm takes its rise, vid., <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference> : on the contrary it cannot be Solomon, because in his reign, though troubled towards its close (1Ki 11:14.), no such event occurs, but would then have to be inferred to have happened from this Psalm. We might rather guess at Uzziah (Meier) or Hezekiah (Maurer), both of whom inherited the kingdom in a weakened condition and found the neighbouring peoples alienated from the house of David. The situation might correspond to these times, for the rebellious peoples, which are brought before us, have been hitherto subject to Jahve and His Anointed. But all historical indications which might support the one supposition or the other are wanting. If the God-anointed one, who speaks in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Psa 2:7</reference>, were the psalmist himself, we should at least know the Psalm was composed by a king filled with a lofty Messianic consciousness. But the dramatic movement of the Psalm up to the ועתה (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.10">Psa 2:10</reference>) which follows, is opposed to such an identification of the God-anointed one with the poet. But that Alexander Jannaeus (Hitz.), that blood-thirsty ruler, so justly hated by his people, who inaugurated his reign by fratricide, may be both at the same time, is a supposition which turns the moral and covenant character of the Psalm into detestable falsehood. The Old Testament knows no kingship to which is promised the dominion of the world and to which sonship is ascribed (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2Sa 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.28">Psa 89:28</reference>), but the Davidic. The events of his own time, which influenced the mind of the poet, are no longer clear to us. But from these he is carried away into those tumults of the peoples which shall end in all kingdoms becoming the kingdom of God and of His Christ (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Rev 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.10">Rev 12:10</reference>). <div eID="gen9042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9043" type="x-p"/> In the New Testament this Psalm is cited more frequently than any other. According to <reference osisRef="Acts.4.25-Acts.4.28">Act 4:25-28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.1">Act 4:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Acts.4.2">Act 4:2</reference> have been fulfilled in the confederate hostility of Israel and the Gentiles against Jesus the holy servant of God and against His confessors. In the Epistle to the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1-Ps.110.7">Psa 110:1-7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12">Psa 2:1-12</reference> stand side by side, the former as a witness of the eternal priesthood of Jesus after the order of Melchisedek, the latter as a witness of His sonship, which is superior to that of the angels. Paul teaches us in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">Act 13:33</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Rom 1:4</reference>, how the “to-day” is to be understood. The “to-day” according to its proper fulfilment, is the day of Jesus’ resurrection. Born from the dead to the life at the right hand of God, He entered on this day, which the church therefore calls <hi type="italic">dies regalis</hi>, upon His eternal kingship. <div eID="gen9043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9044" type="x-p"/> The New Testament echo of this Psalm however goes still deeper and further. The two names of the future One in use in the time of Jesus, ὁ Χριστὸς and ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, Joh 1:50; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.63">Mat 26:63</reference> (in the mouth of Nathanael and of the High Priest) refer back to this Ps. and <reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Dan 9:25</reference>, just as ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου incontrovertibly refers to <reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference> and Dan 7:13. The view maintained by De Wette and Hupfeld, that the Psalm is not applicable to the Christian conceptions of the Messiah, seems almost as though these were to be gauged according to the authoritative utterances of the professorial chair and not according to the language of the Apostles. Even in the Apocalypse, Ps 19:15; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.5">Psa 12:5</reference>, Jesus appears exactly as this Psalm represents Him, as ποιμαίνων τὰ ἔθνη ἐν ῥάβδῳ σιδηρᾷ. The office of the Messiah is not only that of Saviour but also of Judge. Redemption is the beginning and the judgment the end of His work. It is to this end that the Psalm refers. The Lord himself frequently refers in the Gospels to the fact of His bearing side by side with the sceptre of peace and the shepherd’s staff, the sceptre of iron also, Mat 24:50., <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mat 21:44</reference>, Luk 19:27. The day of His coming is indeed a day of judgment-the great day of the ὀργὴ τοῦ ἀγνίου, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.17">Rev 6:17</reference>, before which the ultra-spiritual Messianic creations of enlightened exegetes will melt away, just as the carnal Messianic hopes of the Jews did before His first coming.
entries.a51adab8cb73a4f5de5c890c825a9027b582c060: <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3">Psa 2:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9045" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins with a seven line strophe, ruled by an interrogative Wherefore. The mischievous undertaking condemns itself, It is groundless and fruitless.
